summary: This document defines the exact subset of the Babel routing protocol and its extensions that a Homenet protocol suite implementation needs, and the interactions between the Home Networking Control Protocol (HNCP) and Babel.

eli5.summary: A home network is a tiny version of the Internet. This document picks the parts of the Babel routing program a home network needs and explains how it works with the home setup program.

questions: what is the homenet babel profile
what link costs should babel use for wireless
subtitle: Which parts of Babel a home network router must implement, and how HNCP tells Babel what to announce.

tldr.problem: Babel is flexible and has many optional parts, so routers from different vendors in a home network might pick incompatible options and fail to exchange a full set of routes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists numbered requirements (REQ1 to REQ9) and optional features (OPT1 to OPT4): which Babel features to implement, how to set link costs, and which routes an HNCP node must make Babel announce.
tldr.outcome: Routers following the profile interoperate in a Homenet. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9080 is a Proposed Standard from August 2021. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8966 and RFC 9079.

sections.title: Purpose and Background
sections.content:
The core of the Homenet protocol suite is the Home Networking Control Protocol (HNCP, RFC 7788), which floods configuration information and assigns prefixes to links, combined with the Babel routing protocol (RFC 8966). Babel is extensible and modular: minimal implementations of a few hundred lines of code exist, while the "large" implementation consists of over ten thousand lines of C.

This document has two parts. The first specifies the exact subset of Babel and its extensions that a Homenet implementation requires. The second specifies how HNCP interacts with Babel.

RFC 8966 lets control data travel over link-local IPv6 or IPv4 and leaves link cost, metric computation and route selection to the implementation. Distinct implementations still keep loop-free forwarding paths, but conflicting options could mean they do not exchange a full set of routes, and conflicting route selection could cause persistent oscillations. The profile removes these choices.
sections.eli5: Babel lets each maker choose lots of settings. This document picks the settings for home routers so they all speak the same way.

sections.title: Required Babel Features
sections.content:
Six requirements cover Babel itself:

  • REQ1: control traffic MUST be carried in IPv6 packets to port 6696, using either the multicast group ff02::1:6 or a link-local unicast address.
  • REQ2: MUST implement the IPv6 subset of RFC 8966.
  • REQ3: SHOULD implement the IPv4 subset. Techniques such as multiple layers of NAT are strongly discouraged.
  • REQ4: MUST implement source-specific routing for IPv6 as defined in RFC 9079. IPv4 source-specific routing is not required, because HNCP arranges a single nonspecific IPv4 default route.

The rationale for IPv6 transport is that link-local addresses are properly scoped and reasonably stable, which makes implementations simpler and more reliable.
sections.eli5: Every home router must speak the IPv6 version, should also speak the IPv4 version, and must understand the sender-aware routes from the companion document.

sections.title: Link Costs and Wireless Links
sections.content:
REQ5 asks for metrics of a similar magnitude to those suggested in Appendix A of RFC 8966. An implementation SHOULD assign costs of no less than 256 to wireless links and between 32 and 196 to lossless wired links. Otherwise, mixing routers from different vendors would give suboptimal routing.

REQ6 says an implementation SHOULD distinguish wired from wireless links, assume wireless when it cannot tell, and dynamically probe the quality of wireless links to derive a metric. The rationale quotes the saying that "hop-count routing is worst-path routing": without quality-based metrics, the protocol prefers long, lossy links to shorter, lossless ones. Link-quality estimation is not required for wired links, since it is hard to detect some kinds (such as power-line networks) and no published algorithms are known for them.
sections.eli5: Wi-Fi hops are shakier than cables, so a router should treat them as more expensive and pick the road that really works best, not just the one with fewest stops.

sections.title: Optional Babel Features
sections.content:
Two optional features are listed. OPT1: a node MAY apply hysteresis to route metrics when selecting routes, as suggested in Section 3.6 of RFC 8966, but it is not required and the node may simply pick the smallest metric. Hysteresis is only useful in congested and highly dynamic networks, not in a typical stable, uncongested home network.

OPT2: a node may support other extensions, as long as they are known to interoperate with both the core protocol and source-specific routing. Other extensions are useful in specific situations such as global-scale overlay networks or multi-hop wireless networks with several radio frequencies, so apart from source-specific routing none is required.
sections.eli5: A few extras are allowed but not needed, because a calm home network does not need fancy tricks.

sections.title: How HNCP Drives Babel
sections.content:
The Homenet architecture separates configuration, done by HNCP, from routing, done by Babel. Every interaction consists of HNCP causing Babel to announce something on its behalf; Babel never causes HNCP to act. How this is done is an implementation detail. In existing implementations, HNCP installs a route in the operating system's kernel, and Babel picks it up through its usual redistribution mechanisms.

Three requirements follow:

  • REQ7: if a node receives a DHCPv6 prefix delegation for prefix P and publishes an External-Connection TLV with a Delegated-Prefix TLV for P and no Prefix-Policy TLV, it MUST announce a source-specific default route with source prefix P over Babel.
  • REQ8: if a node gets a DHCPv4 lease and wins the election for NAT gateway, it MUST act as a NAT gateway and MUST announce a nonspecific IPv4 default route.
  • REQ9: if a node assigns prefix P to an attached link and announces it in an Assigned-Prefix TLV, it MUST announce a route towards P over Babel.

Connections with nontrivial prefix policies are excluded from REQ7 because their behaviour is application specific.
sections.eli5: The setup program tells the routing program what to shout to the neighbours, never the other way round. Each new address range or exit to the Internet gets announced.

sections.title: Optional HNCP Interactions
sections.content:
OPT3: a node that receives a DHCPv6 prefix delegation MAY also announce a nonspecific IPv6 default route in addition to the source-specific one required by REQ7. The source-specific route overrides it when all nodes support source-specific routing, and the extra route may help when interoperating with a routing protocol that lacks that support.

OPT4: a NAT gateway node with a DHCPv4 lease SHOULD NOT announce a source-specific IPv4 default route. Doing so causes no blackholes or routing loops, but packets from different parts of the Homenet might follow different paths, with confusing results.
sections.eli5: A router may also announce a plain "anywhere else" road, but for the old-style addresses it should not use sender-specific roads, since that would be confusing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
HNCP and Babel carry control data in IPv6 packets with a link-local source address, and implementations are required to drop packets sent from a global address. They are therefore only exposed to attacks from a directly connected link where they are listening.

Security relies on "Internal", "Ad Hoc" and "Hybrid" interfaces being connected to links secured at a lower layer; packets are only accepted from these. Packets received on "External" and "Guest" interfaces are ignored, as are those on "Leaf" interfaces. So the network depends on the reliability of border discovery in RFC 7788.

Using untrusted links for transit is NOT RECOMMENDED, and any HNCP and Babel traffic over them MUST be secured with an upper-layer security protocol. Both protocols support cryptographic authentication, but no protocol for autonomous configuration of their security had been defined at the time of writing. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Routers only listen to neighbours on trusted wires inside the house and ignore anything arriving from outside doors.
